Kinetic interacting particles

Kinetic Interacting Particle Langevin Monte Carlo

KIPLMC1 from the shared exponential integrator; KIPLMC2 from OBABO.

Published source; checked diffusion and sampler proofs

The comparison uses the supplied KIPLMC main.tex and its sections, including the OBABO rate that depends on the particle number. KIPLMC1 is the kinetic exponential integrator applied to the scaled particle potential, with correlated Gaussian increments represented by a Cholesky factor. KIPLMC2 uses the OOO-BBB-AAA-BBB-OOO splitting. The results prove diffusion convergence in physical time, Gibbs invariance, root mean square parameter estimates for both Gaussian recursions, time-rescaling identities, concentration about the marginal maximizer, and iteration counts. The logistic example is checked analytically. The OBABO argument proves a stronger estimate and then deduces the stated coarser rate with a uniform constant. The continuous solutions are continuous in L2L^2L2. Numerical experiments are reported separately from these estimates.

  • Paul Valsecchi Oliva and Ö. Deniz Akyildiz (2026). Kinetic interacting particle Langevin Monte Carlo. Statistics and Computing 36, article 221. arXiv
  • Arnak S. Dalalyan and Lionel Riou-Durand (2020). On sampling from a log-concave density using kinetic Langevin diffusions. Bernoulli 26(3), 1956–1988. arXiv
  • Pierre Monmarché (2021). High-dimensional MCMC with a standard splitting scheme for the underdamped Langevin diffusion. Electronic Journal of Statistics 15(2), 4117–4166. Full paper

The Brownian KIPLD convergence proposition and both Gaussian algorithm parameter-error theorems are proved. KIPLMC1 reuses the shared exponential integrator; KIPLMC2 has an internal OBABO contraction and Gibbs sampling proof. The source audit records the exact correspondence and source corrections.

Theorems

Convergence of the KIPLD parameter distribution

Mathematical statement

Let N≥1N\ge1N≥1, and suppose the joint potential U(θ,x)U(\theta,x)U(θ,x) is differentiable, mmm-strongly convex, and has LLL-Lipschitz gradient, with 0<m≤L0<m\le L0<m≤L. Initialize the scaled position Z0∼νZ_0\sim\nuZ0​∼ν with finite second moment. Independently initialize scaled velocity as N(0,N−1I)\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)N(0,N−1I), and use the independent Brownian source. If γ2≥m+L\gamma^2\ge m+Lγ2≥m+L, the constructed physical KIPLD parameter law satisfies

W2(L(Θt),πΘ)≤2e−mt/γ(E∥Z0−Zˉ∗∥2)1/2.\boxed{W_2(\mathcal L(\Theta_t),\pi_\Theta)\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\bigl(\mathbb E\|Z_0-\bar Z_*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}.}W2​(L(Θt​),πΘ​)≤2​e−mt/γ(E∥Z0​−Zˉ∗​∥2)1/2.​

Here Zˉ∗∼πZ\bar Z_*\sim\pi_ZZˉ∗​∼πZ​ is independent of Z0Z_0Z0​, and πZ(dz)∝e−VN(z)dz\pi_Z(dz)\propto e^{-V_N(z)}dzπZ​(dz)∝e−VN​(z)dz. The target parameter marginal is exactly πΘ(dθ)∝ℓ(θ)Ndθ\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\propto\ell(\theta)^N d\thetaπΘ​(dθ)∝ℓ(θ)Ndθ. This is the supplied manuscript’s continuous convergence proposition.

The proof applies the earlier kinetic Gibbs-mixing theorem (see Kinetic, Section 3.58.4) with c=Nc=\sqrt Nc=N​, unit-temperature friction cγc\gammacγ, and time t/ct/ct/c. The sum potential has curvature NmNmNm, so its mixing exponent becomes (Nm)/(cγ) (t/c)=mt/γ(Nm)/(c\gamma)\,(t/c)=mt/\gamma(Nm)/(cγ)(t/c)=mt/γ. The flow is rescaled in velocity only; its position endpoint is unchanged. A separate theorem verifies its full physical integral equation and its independent thermal initial law. The earlier Brownian clock-scaling theorem proves that the transformed forcing has amplitude 2γ/N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}2γ/N​ (see Kinetic, Section 3.105.1, Kinetic, Section 3.105.2). Projection to the parameter cannot increase a coupling’s cost, and the independent initial coupling gives the displayed constant.

This statement bounds transport to the powered parameter marginal, rather than distance to its maximizer. To obtain parameter RMS error around the maximizer, one subsequently adds the sharp equilibrium concentration radius from the earlier proximal report (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1). Time reduces the displayed transport term, while particle count controls that additional statistical radius.

The KIPLMC1 parameter root-mean-square error

Mathematical statement

Use the same assumptions and thermal initialization as above. Let θ∗\theta_*θ∗​ be the unique marginal-likelihood maximizer. KIPLMC1 calls the shared Dalalyan–Riou-Durand exponential step with the correlated Gaussian velocity–position innovations. If

γ2≥m+L,0<h,4γLh≤m,\gamma^2\ge m+L,\qquad 0<h,\qquad4\gamma Lh\le m,γ2≥m+L,0<h,4γLh≤m,

Then its parameter iterates obey

(E∥Θn−θ∗∥2)1/2≤C1qn+hC2+dθNm,\boxed{\bigl(\mathbb E\|\Theta_n-\theta_*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\le C_1q^n+hC_2+\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}},}(E∥Θn​−θ∗​∥2)1/2≤C1​qn+hC2​+Nmdθ​​​,​ q=1−3mh4γ,C1=2(E∥Z0−Zˉ∗∥2)1/2,q=1-\frac{3mh}{4\gamma},\qquad C_1=\sqrt2\bigl(\mathbb E\|Z_0-\bar Z_*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2},q=1−4γ3mh​,C1​=2​(E∥Z0​−Zˉ∗​∥2)1/2, C2=2Lmdθ+NdxN.C_2=\frac{\sqrt2L}{m}\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta+Nd_x}{N}}.C2​=m2​L​Ndθ​+Ndx​​​.

The three terms have different meanings. The first depends on initialization and vanishes geometrically. The second is the numerical bias and decreases with the step. The third is the statistical concentration radius and decreases with particle count. Increasing the number of iterations cannot remove either persistent error term.

The proof transfers the exact Gaussian Markov law through the clock and velocity conjugacy, applies the constructed first-order KLMC theorem from the earlier kinetic report (see Kinetic, Section 3.57.19), and checks every power of NNN. The factor NLNLNL from smoothness, the transformed step h/Nh/\sqrt Nh/N​, and curvature NmNmNm leave precisely h(L/m)2(dθ+Ndx)/Nh(L/m)\sqrt{2(d_\theta+Nd_x)/N}h(L/m)2(dθ​+Ndx​)/N​. The earlier nonexpansive parameter projection and projected-RMS transport results (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.1.6, ULA-SC, Section 3.48.9) add the sharp equilibrium radius (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1). The independent initial coupling bounds the initial Wasserstein distance. Gaussian laws, their independence, target invariance, and finite transport moments are proved internally.

The discretization term depends on the thermal dimension factor dx+dθ/Nd_x+d_\theta/Ndx​+dθ​/N. The equilibrium parameter contribution decreases as N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2, while the latent part of the discretization term remains at fixed step. Consequently increasing particle count alone cannot drive the total parameter error to zero.

KIPLMC2: the supplied rate with an explicit uniform constant

Mathematical statement

KIPLMC2 uses the shared O−B−A−B−O\mathrm O-\mathrm B-\mathrm A-\mathrm B-\mathrm OO−B−A−B−O composition with independent Gaussian thermostat vectors. Under the same joint potential assumptions and thermal initialization, suppose

γ>0,γ2≥4L,0<h,33γ3h≤m.\gamma>0,\qquad \gamma^2\ge4L,\qquad0<h,\qquad33\gamma^3h\le m.γ>0,γ2≥4L,0<h,33γ3h≤m.

Put dz=dθ+Ndxd_z=d_\theta+Nd_xdz​=dθ​+Ndx​ and D0=W2(ν,πZ)D_0=W_2(\nu,\pi_Z)D0​=W2​(ν,πZ​). The supplied manuscript’s bound holds with the following explicit constant, independent of N,n,h,dθ,dxN,n,h,d_\theta,d_xN,n,h,dθ​,dx​:

C=2+62γm(4L+Lm66γ3)+1m.C=\sqrt2+\frac{6\sqrt2\gamma}{m}\left(4\sqrt L+\frac{Lm}{66\gamma^3}\right)+\frac1{\sqrt m}.C=2​+m62​γ​(4L​+66γ3Lm​)+m​1​. (E∥Θn−θ∗∥2)1/2≤C[(ND0+hNdz)e−mhn/(6γ)+hNdz+dθ/N].\boxed{\begin{aligned}(\mathbb E\|\Theta_n-\theta_*\|^2)^{1/2}\le C\bigl[&(\sqrt N D_0+hN\sqrt{d_z})e^{-mhn/(6\gamma)}\\&+h\sqrt{Nd_z}+\sqrt{d_\theta/N}\bigr].\end{aligned}}(E∥Θn​−θ∗​∥2)1/2≤C[​(N​D0​+hNdz​​)e−mhn/(6γ)+hNdz​​+dθ​/N​].​​

The proof first applies the stronger position sampling bound from the earlier kinetic report (see Kinetic, Section 3.123.3). In the weighted phase metric, the two-force OBABO step contracts by r=1−mh/(3γ)r=\sqrt{1-mh/(3\gamma)}r=1−mh/(3γ)​. Compare one such step with an exact O\mathrm OO–Hamiltonian–O\mathrm OO step, which preserves the proved Gibbs target. The common-noise local defect is quadratic in hhh; summing the contractive perturbations gives the persistent position bias

62γm hdzN(4L+Lh2).\frac{6\sqrt2\gamma}{m}\,h\sqrt{\frac{d_z}{N}}\left(4\sqrt L+\frac{Lh}{2}\right).m62​γ​hNdz​​​(4L​+2Lh​).

This argument proves sampling from the Gaussian chain directly. It requires no assumed discrete invariant law or external OBABO error estimate. Exact clock scaling and rn≤e−mhn/(6γ)r^n\le e^{-mhn/(6\gamma)}rn≤e−mhn/(6γ) turn that stronger result into the supplied coarse rate, retaining both of its transient terms. The final concentration term is the same sharp statistical contribution from the earlier proximal report as for KIPLMC1 (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1). The accuracy corollaries give positive step choices, natural particle counts, and rounded logarithmic iteration counts.

The constant is uniform in particle count and dimensions because the admissible step cap bounds its remaining step dependence using only curvature and friction. The displayed coarse particle dependence is a consequence of enlarging the sharper thermal bound. Its additional transient contribution decays and does not alter the equilibrium concentration term.

Sharp concentration of the powered parameter marginal

Mathematical statement

Let N≥1N\ge1N≥1 and let the joint potential U:Rdθ+dx→RU:\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\to\mathbb RU:Rdθ​+dx​→R be differentiable and mmm-strongly convex, with m>0m>0m>0. The dimensions dθ,dxd_\theta,d_xdθ​,dx​ may differ and may be zero. Define

ℓ(θ)=∫e−U(θ,x)dx,\ell(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}dx,ℓ(θ)=∫e−U(θ,x)dx, πΘ(dθ)∝ℓ(θ)Ndθ.\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\propto\ell(\theta)^N d\theta.πΘ​(dθ)∝ℓ(θ)Ndθ.

The normalization is positive and finite. The earlier marginal strong-convexity and maximizer theorem gives a unique maximizer θ⋆\theta_\starθ⋆​ of ℓ\ellℓ (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.12.4). The sharp powered-marginal concentration theorem from the proximal report (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1) gives

∫∥θ−θ⋆∥2dπΘ(θ)≤dθNm.\boxed{\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2d\pi_\Theta(\theta) \le\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}.}∫∥θ−θ⋆​∥2dπΘ​(θ)≤Nmdθ​​.​

This gives the sharp concentration contribution dθ/(Nm)\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}dθ​/(Nm)​ in both particle bounds. The exact powered Gibbs target, its kinetic invariance, and both complete numerical error bounds are proved in the supporting modules.

The negative log marginal is strongly convex after latent integration, and powering the marginal likelihood multiplies this curvature by particle count. The moment estimate then has numerator exactly the parameter dimension. This sharp coefficient is carried unchanged into both numerical particle error theorems.

The KIPLMC1 exponential update

Mathematical statement

Write z=(θ,x1/N,…,xN/N)z=(\theta,x^1/\sqrt N,\ldots,x^N/\sqrt N)z=(θ,x1/N​,…,xN/N​), and scale velocities the same way. Put VN(z)=∑iU(θ,Nzi)V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)VN​(z)=∑i​U(θ,N​zi​) and FN=∇VN/NF_N=\nabla V_N/NFN​=∇VN​/N. KIPLMC1 uses the exponential update from the earlier kinetic report (see Kinetic, Section 3.12.1) with force FNF_NFN​ and phase noise amplitude 2γ/N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}2γ/N​:

v+=ψ0(h)v−ψ1(h)FN(z)+2γ/N ε,z+=z+ψ1(h)v−ψ2(h)FN(z)+2γ/N ε′.\begin{aligned} v^+&=\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F_N(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\varepsilon,\\ z^+&=z+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F_N(z)+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\varepsilon'. \end{aligned}v+z+​=ψ0​(h)v−ψ1​(h)FN​(z)+2γ/N​ε,=z+ψ1​(h)v−ψ2​(h)FN​(z)+2γ/N​ε′.​

After multiplying a latent coordinate by N\sqrt NN​, its velocity update is precisely

Vxi,+=ψ0(h)Vxi−ψ1(h)∇xU(θ,xi)+2γ εi.V^{x_i,+}=\psi_0(h)V^{x_i}-\psi_1(h)\nabla_xU(\theta,x^i) +\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\varepsilon^i.Vxi​,+=ψ0​(h)Vxi​−ψ1​(h)∇x​U(θ,xi)+2γ​εi.

The coordinate identity follows by differentiating the lifted potential and undoing the latent spatial scale. The same response coefficients govern both parameter and latent coordinates.

The parameter counterpart uses the particle-average gradient and thermal amplitude 2γ/N\sqrt{2\gamma/N}2γ/N​. Both parameter and latent position updates integrate their corresponding velocity responses using the same correlated innovation block. These coordinate identities therefore specify the full common exponential algorithm in physical variables.

The KIPLMC2 OBABO update

Mathematical statement

Set δ=e−γh/2\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}δ=e−γh/2, σ=(1−δ2)/N\sigma=\sqrt{(1-\delta^2)/N}σ=(1−δ2)/N​, and take separate noise vectors ξ,ξ′\xi,\xi'ξ,ξ′ for thermostat half-steps. KIPLMC2 is exactly

v1/2=δv+σξ−h2FN(z),z+=z+hv1/2,v+=δ(v1/2−h2FN(z+))+σξ′.v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma\xi-\tfrac h2F_N(z),\qquad z^+=z+hv_{1/2},\qquad v^+=\delta\bigl(v_{1/2}-\tfrac h2F_N(z^+)\bigr)+\sigma\xi'.v1/2​=δv+σξ−2h​FN​(z),z+=z+hv1/2​,v+=δ(v1/2​−2h​FN​(z+))+σξ′.

The new position is used when recomputing the second force. These are the five subflows of the earlier kinetic splitting identity (see Kinetic, Section 3.20.1), composed in the displayed order. The parameter coordinates use the average pair gradient, while undoing latent scaling gives the individual pair gradients and ordinary latent thermal amplitude.

The two thermostat vectors are independent standard Gaussians and independent of the current state. Their amplitudes give covariance I/NI/NI/N in scaled equilibrium velocity. Multiplying latent position and velocity by N\sqrt NN​ recovers the individual pair-gradient kick and unit-temperature latent refresh.

The mathematical argument

The argument below gives the estimates in order, including their constants and analytic justification. The adjacent panels identify the corresponding checked Lean statements and explain their role in the proof.

01The likelihood and interacting latent particles §

The observation yyy is fixed. A model gives a joint density pθ(x,y)p_\theta(x,y)pθ​(x,y), but the quantity to optimize is its integral over an unobserved variable:

pθ(y)=∫pθ(x,y)dx,θ∗=arg⁡max⁡θlog⁡pθ(y).p_\theta(y)=\int p_\theta(x,y)dx, \qquad\theta_*=\arg\max_\theta\log p_\theta(y).pθ​(y)=∫pθ​(x,y)dx,θ∗​=argθmax​logpθ​(y).

Computing this integral and its gradient exactly can be difficult. The particle method retains NNN latent states X1,…,XNX^1,\ldots,X^NX1,…,XN, coupled through the same parameter θ\thetaθ. The force on the parameter is the average of the parameter gradients, while the latent drift uses the corresponding latent gradient:

Fθ=1N∑i=1N∇θU(θ,Xi),Fxi=∇xU(θ,Xi).F^\theta=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\nabla_\theta U(\theta,X^i), \qquad F^{x_i}=\nabla_xU(\theta,X^i).Fθ=N1​i=1∑N​∇θ​U(θ,Xi),Fxi​=∇x​U(θ,Xi).

Adding a parameter noise of size N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2 makes the whole system a Langevin system with an explicit Gibbs equilibrium. The particle number then has two roles: it provides interacting latent samples and determines how strongly the stationary parameter distribution concentrates near the optimizer.

The common parameter is represented once while each latent variable has its own coordinate. Conditional on that parameter, the equilibrium latent integrations factor into identical marginal likelihood integrals. Increasing particle count changes the parameter density by increasing the power of the likelihood, and increases the state dimension linearly.

The unique MMLE and exact powered parameter marginal are proved for the normalized target.

02Joint strong convexity and smoothness of the statistical potential §

The source paper assumes U∈C2U\in C^2U∈C2, μ>0\mu>0μ>0, L>0L>0L>0, and

⟨z−z′,∇U(z)−∇U(z′)⟩≥μ∥z−z′∥2,∥∇U(z)−∇U(z′)∥≤L∥z−z′∥,\langle z-z',\nabla U(z)-\nabla U(z')\rangle \ge\mu\|z-z'\|^2,\qquad \|\nabla U(z)-\nabla U(z')\|\le L\|z-z'\|,⟨z−z′,∇U(z)−∇U(z′)⟩≥μ∥z−z′∥2,∥∇U(z)−∇U(z′)∥≤L∥z−z′∥,

Here z=(θ,x)z=(\theta,x)z=(θ,x). The proved convergence bounds require differentiability and the displayed gradient inequalities. Under the source’s additional twice-continuous-differentiability assumption, these inequalities are equivalent to μI⪯∇2U(z)⪯LI\mu I\preceq\nabla^2U(z)\preceq LIμI⪯∇2U(z)⪯LI. Thus μ≤L\mu\le Lμ≤L in positive dimension. Strong convexity in xxx with θ\thetaθ fixed does not imply joint strong convexity: the lower bound must also hold in directions that change both variables.

The paper's unregularized logistic example illustrates the distinction. Its Gaussian prior contributes a quadratic in x−θx-\thetax−θ, which leaves common shifts partly uncontrolled; logistic curvature can vanish far from the origin. Spanning covariates give strict convexity, while a uniform positive strong-convexity constant requires additional regularization. The source itself separates these experiments from its strong-convexity theorem.

The required lower curvature concerns arbitrary joint directions (u,w)(u,w)(u,w), including directions that move parameter and latent variables together. Positive curvature in either coordinate with the other fixed is insufficient. A direction in which both move can remove a prior penalty and expose weak or vanishing curvature in the likelihood.

The finite-observation logistic potential has the exact source gradient, block Hessian, global Lipschitz constant, convexity, and full-span strict convexity. Its failure of positive global joint strong convexity in a nontrivial space is proved, rather than inferred from strict convexity. The experimental example therefore has exactly the source’s stated assumption caveat.

03The kinetic particle equations in physical coordinates §

KIPLD adds velocity blocks Vθ,VxiV^\theta,V^{x_i}Vθ,Vxi​ and uses the same friction in each:

dθ=Vθdt,dXi=Vxidt,d\theta=V^\theta dt,\qquad dX^i=V^{x_i}dt,dθ=Vθdt,dXi=Vxi​dt, dVθ=−(γVθ+Fθ)dt+2γ/N dB0,dVxi=−(γVxi+Fxi)dt+2γ dBi.dV^\theta=-(\gamma V^\theta+F^\theta)dt +\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,dB^0, \quad dV^{x_i}=-(\gamma V^{x_i}+F^{x_i})dt+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,dB^i.dVθ=−(γVθ+Fθ)dt+2γ/N​dB0,dVxi​=−(γVxi​+Fxi​)dt+2γ​dBi.

The Brownian blocks are independent. The parameter velocity has equilibrium covariance N−1IN^{-1}IN−1I; every latent velocity has covariance III. These scales are chosen together with the average parameter force. Changing one without changing the others generally changes the equilibrium target.

The noise acts on velocity, while positions are integrals of velocities. This creates the smoother position paths responsible for the exponential integrator's improved discretization dependence. The target remains a statistical estimation problem: the final parameter distribution should concentrate around θ∗\theta_*θ∗​ as the particle number grows.

The parameter noise is reduced by the square root of particle count, matching its averaged force and concentrated equilibrium marginal. Each physical latent equation retains unit temperature. Scaling all latent positions and velocities by N−1/2N^{-1/2}N−1/2 turns these different physical amplitudes into one uniform phase-space temperature.

The constructed Brownian physical-time flow satisfies the exact particle integral equation and has the required independent thermal initialization.

04Transformation to unit-temperature kinetic coordinates §

The particle system looks anisotropic, but it becomes a standard kinetic system in dz=dθ+Ndxd_z=d_\theta+Nd_xdz​=dθ​+Ndx​ dimensions. At rescaled time ttt, define

Z~t=(θNt,N−1/2XNt1,…),V~t=(NVNtθ,VNtx1,…).\widetilde Z_t=(\theta_{\sqrt Nt},N^{-1/2}X^1_{\sqrt Nt},\ldots), \qquad\widetilde V_t=(\sqrt N V^\theta_{\sqrt Nt},V^{x_1}_{\sqrt Nt},\ldots).Zt​=(θN​t​,N−1/2XN​t1​,…),Vt​=(N​VN​tθ​,VN​tx1​​,…).

Set

UˉN(θ,z1,…,zN)=1N∑i=1NU(θ,Nzi),fN=NUˉN,γ~=Nγ.\bar U_N(\theta,z_1,\ldots,z_N)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i), \qquad f_N=N\bar U_N,\qquad\widetilde\gamma=\sqrt N\gamma.UˉN​(θ,z1​,…,zN​)=N1​i=1∑N​U(θ,N​zi​),fN​=NUˉN​,γ​=N​γ.

Brownian scaling produces independent standard blocks B~ti=N−1/4BNti\widetilde B_t^i=N^{-1/4}B^i_{\sqrt Nt}Bti​=N−1/4BN​ti​. Direct substitution yields

dZ~t=V~tdt,dV~t=−(γ~V~t+∇fN(Z~t))dt+2γ~ dB~t.d\widetilde Z_t=\widetilde V_tdt,\qquad d\widetilde V_t=-(\widetilde\gamma\widetilde V_t+\nabla f_N(\widetilde Z_t))dt +\sqrt{2\widetilde\gamma}\,d\widetilde B_t.dZt​=Vt​dt,dVt​=−(γ​Vt​+∇fN​(Zt​))dt+2γ​​dBt​.

This is Proposition A.1. The parameter position stays unchanged under the spatial scaling, which will make projection of the final transport estimate particularly simple. An original step η\etaη corresponds to a rescaled step η~=η/N\widetilde\eta=\eta/\sqrt Nη​=η/N​.

The latent spatial scaling is applied first. The subsequent velocity and clock transformation fixes these scaled position coordinates. The parameter position is unchanged throughout. Friction and step are changed inversely, preserving their dimensionless product. The normalized Gaussian velocity and transformed Brownian amplitude must be transformed together; a deterministic clock identity alone would not identify the sampler’s probability law.

The drift, complete integral equation, Brownian scaling, independent coordinates, and endpoint law all transform with the exact particle clock.

05Curvature and smoothness of the scaled particle potential §

The gradients of the averaged potential are

∇θUˉN=1N∑i∇θU(θ,Nzi),∇ziUˉN=1N∇xU(θ,Nzi).\nabla_\theta\bar U_N=\frac1N\sum_i\nabla_\theta U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i), \qquad\nabla_{z_i}\bar U_N=\frac1{\sqrt N}\nabla_xU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i).∇θ​UˉN​=N1​i∑​∇θ​U(θ,N​zi​),∇zi​​UˉN​=N​1​∇x​U(θ,N​zi​).

Apply the lifted strong-convexity theorem from the earlier particle geometry report (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.1.3). Equivalently, apply joint strong convexity to each pair (θ,Nzi),(θ′,Nzi′)(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i),(\theta',\sqrt Nz'_i)(θ,N​zi​),(θ′,N​zi′​), divide by NNN, and sum. The repeated parameter term and the scaled latent terms combine exactly:

⟨Z−Z′,∇UˉN(Z)−∇UˉN(Z′)⟩≥μ(∥θ−θ′∥2+∑i∥zi−zi′∥2).\langle Z-Z',\nabla\bar U_N(Z)-\nabla\bar U_N(Z')\rangle \ge\mu\left(\|\theta-\theta'\|^2+\sum_i\|z_i-z'_i\|^2\right).⟨Z−Z′,∇UˉN​(Z)−∇UˉN​(Z′)⟩≥μ(∥θ−θ′∥2+i∑​∥zi​−zi′​∥2).

For smoothness, Jensen bounds the squared norm of the averaged parameter gradient by the average of squared norms. Adding the latent-gradient squares then permits one joint LLL-Lipschitz estimate per particle, giving ∥∇UˉN(Z)−∇UˉN(Z′)∥≤L∥Z−Z′∥\|\nabla\bar U_N(Z)-\nabla\bar U_N(Z')\|\le L\|Z-Z'\|∥∇UˉN​(Z)−∇UˉN​(Z′)∥≤L∥Z−Z′∥. This is the earlier lifted-gradient Lipschitz theorem divided by NNN (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.1.4).

Thus the standard potential fN=NUˉNf_N=N\bar U_NfN​=NUˉN​ has constants mN=Nμm_N=N\mumN​=Nμ, MN=NLM_N=NLMN​=NL. Their ratio is L/μL/\muL/μ, independent of NNN. These identities determine the dependence of the KIPLMC1 error bound on particle count.

The lifted sum potential has curvature and gradient Lipschitz constants multiplied by NNN. Dividing the potential by NNN cancels both factors in physical time. As a result the synchronous rate depends on the original pair constants, while total coordinate dimension appears only through thermal and numerical moments.

The averaged potential has the stated force, curvature and smoothness, independently of particle count.

06The normalized powered-likelihood parameter marginal §

The rescaled kinetic Gibbs density is

Π~(dz,dv)∝exp⁡[−∑iU(θ,Nzi)−12∥v∥2]dz dv.\widetilde\Pi(dz,dv)\propto \exp\left[-\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)-\frac12\|v\|^2\right]dz\,dv.Π(dz,dv)∝exp[−i∑​U(θ,N​zi​)−21​∥v∥2]dzdv.

Integrating the Gaussian velocity gives a constant. For each latent block, substitute xi=Nzix_i=\sqrt Nz_ixi​=N​zi​. Its Jacobian is independent of θ\thetaθ, so it is absorbed in normalization. The earlier exact parameter-marginal theorem identifies the normalized pushforward after the same coordinate change (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.9.9). The remaining product separates:

πΘ(θ)∝∏i=1N∫e−U(θ,xi)dxi=pθ(y)N=e−Nκ(θ),κ=−log⁡pθ(y).\pi_\Theta(\theta)\propto \prod_{i=1}^N\int e^{-U(\theta,x_i)}dx_i =p_\theta(y)^N=e^{-N\kappa(\theta)},\quad \kappa=-\log p_\theta(y).πΘ​(θ)∝i=1∏N​∫e−U(θ,xi​)dxi​=pθ​(y)N=e−Nκ(θ),κ=−logpθ​(y).

At stationarity, more particles therefore sharpen the likelihood density rather than changing its maximizer. The maximizer is unchanged by taking a positive integer power. It relies on the parameter noise being present at the prescribed scale; a noise-free parameter gradient flow has a different invariant structure.

The density computation identifies the candidate marginal. Normalization and finite second moments follow from the earlier lifted-target construction (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.5.1, IPLA-SC, Section 3.5.1). Invariance is a separate dynamical assertion, supplied by the kinetic phase-stationarity theorem after the clock change (see Kinetic, Section 3.58.3).

The latent variables become independent under the conditional Gibbs density for a fixed parameter. Fubini multiplies their identical integrals into ℓ(θ)N\ell(\theta)^Nℓ(θ)N. Dividing by the finite positive full partition function gives the powered marginal, so the concentration argument applies to a normalized probability measure.

Normalization, full kinetic Gibbs stationarity under the standard clock, and the exact parameter marginal are proved.

07The sharp parameter second moment about the maximizer §

Strong Prékopa–Leindler preserves the parameter curvature when the latent variable is integrated out: κ\kappaκ is μ\muμ-strongly convex (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.12.3). Thus its minimizer θ∗\theta_*θ∗​ is unique (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.12.4), and the potential of πΘ\pi_\ThetaπΘ​ has curvature NμN\muNμ.

The sharp moment theorem in the earlier proximal report compares Gibbs partition integrals under dilation toward the minimizer (see Proximal, Section 3.5.2). It requires continuity and strong convexity of the marginal potential, without a differentiability assumption on that potential. Applied to NκN\kappaNκ, and then to the exact powered particle marginal (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1), it gives

W2(πΘ,δθ∗)=(EπΘ∥θ−θ∗∥2)1/2≤dθNμ.W_2(\pi_\Theta,\delta_{\theta_*}) =\bigl(\mathbb E_{\pi_\Theta}\|\theta-\theta_*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2} \le\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{N\mu}}.W2​(πΘ​,δθ∗​​)=(EπΘ​​∥θ−θ∗​∥2)1/2≤Nμdθ​​​.

The coefficient is sharp: an isotropic Gaussian with covariance (Nμ)−1I(N\mu)^{-1}I(Nμ)−1I attains equality. This explains why a proof with an extra 2\sqrt22​ coefficient, although valid, would not reproduce Proposition 2 exactly.

The radius is a root-mean-square statement around the maximizer, rather than a covariance statement around the marginal mean. Its explicit coefficient is important for the final triangle inequality. No equality of the mean and maximizer is required to add this equilibrium contribution to the numerical sampling error.

The normalized powered marginal satisfies the dimension-sharp concentration bound about its unique maximizer.

08Transport to equilibrium and concentration about the maximizer §

The only coupling of a probability law with a point mass fixes the second coordinate, so Wasserstein distance to a point is exactly root mean square error. The triangle inequality gives

(E∥θn−θ∗∥2)1/2≤W2(Law⁡(θn),πΘ)+dθNμ.\bigl(\mathbb E\|\theta_n-\theta_*\|^2\bigr)^{1/2} \le W_2(\operatorname{Law}(\theta_n),\pi_\Theta) +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{N\mu}}.(E∥θn​−θ∗​∥2)1/2≤W2​(Law(θn​),πΘ​)+Nμdθ​​​.

The first term is a numerical sampling error; the second is the equilibrium statistical radius. Increasing nnn reduces the transient sampling error. Decreasing the step reduces discretization bias. Increasing NNN reduces the concentration term. These operations affect different pieces of the bound.

The map from full rescaled position, or full phase space, to its parameter block is 1-Lipschitz. The earlier particle-geometry result gives operator norm at most one for this projection (see IPLA-SC, Section 3.1.6). Applying it to any coupling cannot increase its quadratic transport cost. Therefore a bound on the ordinary kinetic sampler immediately controls the parameter sampling term once the algorithm-law correspondence has been proved.

The projected root-mean-square transport inequality gives the next step (see ULA-SC, Section 3.48.9): for any coupling of the numerical position and an equilibrium position, project both to parameters and use Minkowski’s inequality around the maximizer. The projected discrepancy is bounded by the full scaled-state discrepancy because the projection is nonexpansive. Infimizing the latter cost yields the sampling term plus the equilibrium parameter radius.

The diffusion and both Gaussian chains combine transport and sharp equilibrium concentration by the checked projected L2L^2L2 triangle inequality.

09The KIPLMC1 exponential update and its change of coordinates §

Reuse ψ0,ψ1,ψ2\psi_0,\psi_1,\psi_2ψ0​,ψ1​,ψ2​ and the frozen-force exponential update from the earlier kinetic report (see Kinetic, Section 3.12.1). With fresh correlated Gaussian pairs of covariance CCC, KIPLMC1 updates

θ+=θ+ψ1(η)Vθ−ψ2(η)Fθ+2γ/N ε0′,\theta^+=\theta+\psi_1(\eta)V^\theta-\psi_2(\eta)F^\theta +\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\varepsilon^{0\prime},θ+=θ+ψ1​(η)Vθ−ψ2​(η)Fθ+2γ/N​ε0′, Vθ+=ψ0(η)Vθ−ψ1(η)Fθ+2γ/N ε0.V^{\theta+}=\psi_0(\eta)V^\theta-\psi_1(\eta)F^\theta +\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,\varepsilon^0.Vθ+=ψ0​(η)Vθ−ψ1​(η)Fθ+2γ/N​ε0.

Each latent block uses the same formulas with Xi,Vxi,FxiX^i,V^{x_i},F^{x_i}Xi,Vxi​,Fxi​ and noise scale 2γ\sqrt{2\gamma}2γ​. This is Algorithm 1.

Proposition B.1 proves the correspondence by changing variables in the ordinary exponential step with γ~=Nγ\widetilde\gamma=\sqrt N\gammaγ​=N​γ and η~=η/N\widetilde\eta=\eta/\sqrt Nη​=η/N​. The coefficients obey

ψ~0(η~)=ψ0(η),ψ~1(η~)=N−1/2ψ1(η),ψ~2(η~)=N−1ψ2(η).\widetilde\psi_0(\widetilde\eta)=\psi_0(\eta),\quad \widetilde\psi_1(\widetilde\eta)=N^{-1/2}\psi_1(\eta),\quad \widetilde\psi_2(\widetilde\eta)=N^{-1}\psi_2(\eta).ψ​0​(η​)=ψ0​(η),ψ​1​(η​)=N−1/2ψ1​(η),ψ​2​(η​)=N−1ψ2​(η).

The velocity and position Gaussian integrals scale by N−1/4N^{-1/4}N−1/4 and N−3/4N^{-3/4}N−3/4, respectively. Their covariance entries therefore scale by N−1/2,N−1,N−3/2N^{-1/2},N^{-1},N^{-3/2}N−1/2,N−1,N−3/2. Matching these laws, in addition to matching the deterministic terms, permits reuse of the same kinetic convergence proof.

The parameter force contains a particle mean because the common parameter occurs in every potential summand. A latent force belongs to only one summand. Undoing its spatial scaling cancels the averaging factor, explaining why the physical latent update uses its individual gradient and ordinary thermal amplitude.

KIPLMC1 uses the shared exponential step. Exact correlated-Gaussian and chain-law conjugacies identify its output with the shared kinetic sampler.

mNhNγN=μηγ,MNhNmN2dz=2LμηdθN+dx.\frac{m_Nh_N}{\gamma_N}=\frac{\mu\eta}{\gamma},\qquad \frac{M_Nh_N}{m_N}\sqrt{2d_z} =\sqrt2\frac L\mu\eta\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}N+d_x}.γN​mN​hN​​=γμη​,mN​MN​hN​​2dz​​=2​μL​ηNdθ​​+dx​​.

The linear friction and step restrictions reduce exactly to γ≥μ+L\gamma\ge\sqrt{\mu+L}γ≥μ+L​ and η≤μ/(4γL)\eta\le\mu/(4\gamma L)η≤μ/(4γL). The projected-RMS transport inequality (see ULA-SC, Section 3.48.9) and the sharp particle concentration radius (see Proximal, Section 3.6.1) then give

En≤2D0(1−3μη4γ)n+2LμηdθN+dx+dθNμ.\mathcal E_n\le\sqrt2D_0 \left(1-\frac{3\mu\eta}{4\gamma}\right)^n +\sqrt2\frac L\mu\eta\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}N+d_x} +\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}{N\mu}}.En​≤2​D0​(1−4γ3μη​)n+2​μL​ηNdθ​​+dx​​+Nμdθ​​​.

The initial position Wasserstein distance is a valid D0D_0D0​. The paper instead upper-bounds it by the root mean square distance to an independently sampled stationary position. Initialization must include mutually independent Gaussian velocity blocks, independent of position, so that the rescaled velocity is precisely the standard Gaussian product needed by the shared theorem.

Choosing NNN of order dθ/ε2d_\theta/\varepsilon^2dθ​/ε2 and η\etaη of order ε/dx\varepsilon/\sqrt{d_x}ε/dx​​, subject to stability, bounds both persistent terms. The transient then needs order dx/ε\sqrt{d_x}/\varepsilondx​​/ε steps, up to logarithmic and curvature factors.

The total scaled dimension is D=dθ+NdxD=d_\theta+Nd_xD=dθ​+Ndx​, and thermal variance per coordinate is 1/N1/N1/N. Thus the stationary velocity radius is D/N=dθ/N+dx\sqrt{D/N}=\sqrt{d_\theta/N+d_x}D/N​=dθ​/N+dx​​. This identity is the probabilistic meaning of the particle-factor cancellation in the first-order discretization term.

The complete printed Gaussian RMS theorem and its finite ε\varepsilonε-accuracy corollary are proved, including the independent initial coupling constant.

11The five OBABO substeps §

KIPLMC2 uses the symmetric five-subflow composition established in the earlier kinetic report (see Kinetic, Section 3.20.1). Write OOO for friction plus noise, BBB for the force kick, and AAA for free transport. The composition is

O(η/2)  B(η/2)  A(η)  B(η/2)  O(η/2).O(\eta/2)\;B(\eta/2)\;A(\eta)\;B(\eta/2)\;O(\eta/2).O(η/2)B(η/2)A(η)B(η/2)O(η/2).

Let δ=e−γη/2\delta=e^{-\gamma\eta/2}δ=e−γη/2, s=1−δ2s=\sqrt{1-\delta^2}s=1−δ2​. For a standard velocity block, an OOO half-step is v↦δv+sξv\mapsto\delta v+s\xiv↦δv+sξ; for the parameter block it is Vθ↦δVθ+sξ/NV^\theta\mapsto\delta V^\theta+s\xi/\sqrt NVθ↦δVθ+sξ/N​. A BBB half-step subtracts ηF/2\eta F/2ηF/2, and the full AAA step sends x↦x+ηvx\mapsto x+\eta vx↦x+ηv.

The second BBB kick must use the force at the newly computed position. The last OOO step uses an independent Gaussian vector. Symmetry gives the method its second-order splitting structure, while only first derivatives of UUU are evaluated. This is an entirely different construction from the Hessian-corrected KLMC2 in the first paper.

Each thermostat half step separately preserves the appropriate Gaussian velocity law, each force kick is a velocity translation, and each drift is a position translation. Their order determines which refreshed velocity moves position and where the second nonlinear force is evaluated.

The five-subflow composition and its exact algebraic expansion are proved.

12The expanded OBABO update §

For one standard block with force ggg, combine the first OOO and BBB operations:

v1/2=δv+sξ−η2g(x),x+=x+ηv1/2.v_{1/2}=\delta v+s\xi-\frac\eta2g(x), \qquad x^+=x+\eta v_{1/2}.v1/2​=δv+sξ−2η​g(x),x+=x+ηv1/2​.

Apply the final force kick and OU refresh:

v+=δ(v1/2−η2g(x+))+sξ′=δ2v−ηδ2(g(x)+g(x+))+s(δξ+ξ′).v^+=\delta\left(v_{1/2}-\frac\eta2g(x^+)\right)+s\xi' =\delta^2v-\frac{\eta\delta}2\bigl(g(x)+g(x^+)\bigr) +s(\delta\xi+\xi').v+=δ(v1/2​−2η​g(x+))+sξ′=δ2v−2ηδ​(g(x)+g(x+))+s(δξ+ξ′).

In the parameter block replace ggg by the average FθF^\thetaFθ, and both Gaussian amplitudes by s/Ns/\sqrt Ns/N​. The latent blocks use individual forces and amplitude sss. These identities reproduce Algorithm 2 and Proposition B.2.

The resulting law is determined by two independent standard Gaussian vectors, independent of the current state. Proving the displayed algebra for arbitrary supplied noise vectors verifies the deterministic update; proving the stochastic theorem additionally constructs this Gaussian kernel, its iterates and the required moment estimates.

The final combined noise is s(δξ+ξ′)s(\delta\xi+\xi^{\prime})s(δξ+ξ′), but position depends only on the first refresh through the half velocity. Therefore the full phase output has a nontrivial shared-noise structure even though the two input thermostat vectors are independent. The expanded formula retains this structure exactly.

The coordinate equations use the new-position force and two independent Gaussian thermostat vectors. Their Markov law is constructed.

13Comparison through a discrete invariant measure §

A finite-step OBABO kernel PhP_hPh​ generally has its own invariant law Πh\Pi_hΠh​, different from the kinetic Gibbs law Π\PiΠ. The cited Monmarché analysis supplies phase-space contraction and invariant bias bounds of the form

W2(ρPhn,σPhn)≤Aqn/2W2(ρ,σ),b=W2(Πh,Π)≤B.W_2(\rho P_h^n,\sigma P_h^n)\le A q^{n/2}W_2(\rho,\sigma), \qquad b=W_2(\Pi_h,\Pi)\le B.W2​(ρPhn​,σPhn​)≤Aqn/2W2​(ρ,σ),b=W2​(Πh​,Π)≤B.

Apply the triangle inequality twice, using invariance of Πh\Pi_hΠh​:

W2(ρPhn,Π)≤Aqn/2(W2(ρ,Π)+B)+B.W_2(\rho P_h^n,\Pi) \le A q^{n/2}\bigl(W_2(\rho,\Pi)+B\bigr)+B.W2​(ρPhn​,Π)≤Aqn/2(W2​(ρ,Π)+B)+B.

This explains two different occurrences of the numerical bias: a persistent BBB and a transient Aqn/2BAq^{n/2}BAqn/2B. Dropping the latter would lose a term present in the supplied paper's revised theorem.

These inequalities are substantial results about the OBABO kernel, including existence of Πh\Pi_hΠh​. A theorem that takes them as hypotheses checks the transport combination but does not prove the cited OBABO analysis. The coverage audit distinguishes that conditional use from a completed argument.

A second argument compares the chain with a transition preserving Gibbs and does not require a discrete invariant law. The earlier kinetic report proves that an exact O\mathrm OO–Hamiltonian–O\mathrm OO step preserves the continuous Gibbs target (see Kinetic, Section 3.120.3). Compare it with the OBABO update on the same initial state and the same Gaussian vectors. The Verlet local defect has L2L^2L2 cost of order h2dzh^2\sqrt{d_z}h2dz​​. The earlier kinetic perturbation theorem sums this cost directly over the chain (see Kinetic, Section 3.122.3). The resulting bound with the thermal dimension factor is stronger than the supplied coarse estimate, so it also implies every term retained in the printed theorem.

The proof obtains a stronger direct sampling estimate by comparing OBABO with an exact Gibbs-preserving O\mathrm OO–Hamiltonian–O\mathrm OO step and accumulating its local defect. No discrete invariant-law or external bias theorem is assumed.

14Particle dependence of the OBABO coefficients §

For comparison with the direct bound, the manuscript’s cited discrete-invariant-law analysis uses the following rescaled constants

AN=3max⁡{NL,(NL)−1/2},q=1−μη3γ.A_N=\sqrt3\max\{\sqrt{NL},(NL)^{-1/2}\},\qquad q=1-\frac{\mu\eta}{3\gamma}.AN​=3​max{NL​,(NL)−1/2},q=1−3γμη​.

Under γ≥2L\gamma\ge2\sqrt Lγ≥2L​ and 0<η≤η0=μ/(33γ3)0<\eta\le\eta_0=\mu/(33\gamma^3)0<η≤η0​=μ/(33γ3), one has 0<q<10<q<10<q<1. Write ML=max⁡{L,L−1/2}M_L=\max\{\sqrt L,L^{-1/2}\}ML​=max{L​,L−1/2}. Because N≥1N\ge1N≥1, AN≤3NMLA_N\le\sqrt{3N}M_LAN​≤3N​ML​. The detailed bias expression in the source can be bounded by

BN≤3G∗ηNdz,B_N\le\sqrt3G_*\eta\sqrt{Nd_z},BN​≤3​G∗​ηNdz​​, G∗=6γLμML(1+η0L2μ)(1+eLη02(η06+η02L24)).G_*=\frac{6\gamma L}{\mu}M_L \left(1+\frac{\eta_0L}{2\sqrt\mu}\right) \left(1+e^{L\eta_0^2} \left(\frac{\eta_0}{6}+\frac{\eta_0^2L}{24}\right)\right).G∗​=μ6γL​ML​(1+2μ​η0​L​)(1+eLη02​(6η0​​+24η02​L​)).

All factors increase with a nonnegative step, so evaluating at the fixed upper limit η0\eta_0η0​ removes hidden step dependence. This makes G∗G_*G∗​ a constant depending only on μ,L,γ\mu,L,\gammaμ,L,γ.

The product ANBNA_NB_NAN​BN​ is proportional to ηNdz\eta N\sqrt{d_z}ηNdz​​, while BNB_NBN​ itself is proportional to ηNdz\eta\sqrt{Nd_z}ηNdz​​. The two terms have different powers of NNN, which is why the source tracks them separately before introducing the implicit constant.

The clock changes both curvature constants and friction, while leaving the physical contraction ratio unchanged. Simplifying the bias only after substituting every factor avoids introducing spurious growing powers of NNN. The direct position sampling theorem from the earlier kinetic report instead gives a bound with thermal dimension factor (see Kinetic, Section 3.123.3), which is stronger than the coarser printed bound.

Exact algorithm and Gaussian-law conjugacy cancel the particle clock factors. The smaller thermal discretization term implies the supplied coarse rate with an explicit constant depending only on mmm, LLL and γ\gammaγ.

15The KIPLMC2 bound with both transient terms §

Independent Gaussian initialization gives the same velocity marginal as Π~\widetilde\PiΠ. Coupling these equal velocity blocks and using position projection proves the exact identity

W2(ρ0,Π~)=W2(ν,π~Z)=D0.W_2(\rho_0,\widetilde\Pi) =W_2(\nu,\widetilde\pi_Z)=D_0.W2​(ρ0​,Π)=W2​(ν,πZ​)=D0​.

Insert the scaled AN,BNA_N,B_NAN​,BN​ into the discrete equilibrium comparison, project to θ\thetaθ, and add the concentration radius. With a constant CCC depending only on μ,L,γ\mu,L,\gammaμ,L,γ, the supplied manuscript obtains

En≤C[(ND0+ηNdθ+Ndx)e−μηn/(6γ)+ηN(dθ+Ndx)+dθ/N].\mathcal E_n\le C\left[ \bigl(\sqrt N D_0+\eta N\sqrt{d_\theta+Nd_x}\bigr) e^{-\mu\eta n/(6\gamma)} +\eta\sqrt{N(d_\theta+Nd_x)} +\sqrt{d_\theta/N}\right].En​≤C[(N​D0​+ηNdθ​+Ndx​​)e−μηn/(6γ)+ηN(dθ​+Ndx​)​+dθ​/N​].

The exponential follows from (1−μη/(3γ))n/2≤e−μηn/(6γ)(1-\mu\eta/(3\gamma))^{n/2}\le e^{-\mu\eta n/(6\gamma)}(1−μη/(3γ))n/2≤e−μηn/(6γ). The paper gives an explicit common coefficient by taking the maximum of 3ML,3G∗,3MLG∗\sqrt3M_L,\sqrt3G_*,3M_LG_*3​ML​,3​G∗​,3ML​G∗​ and absorbing the concentration factor μ−1/2\mu^{-1/2}μ−1/2.

This bound has worse particle dependence than the KIPLMC1 bound. The paper regards that dependence as a limitation of the available estimate and compares it with numerical behavior; the experiments do not themselves remove the factor from the theorem.

The extra transient term is harmless for validity but matters when reproducing the displayed manuscript formula. It decays with the same rate as the initial transport discrepancy. The sharper invariant-comparator estimate from the earlier kinetic report bounds the chain directly (see Kinetic, Section 3.123.3) and implies this coarser statement by nonnegative termwise enlargements.

The supplied theorem, including both transient terms, follows for the Gaussian sampler. Positive step, integer particle and rounded iteration prescriptions give a finite ε\varepsilonε guarantee.

16Iteration counts and the scope of the experimental examples §

For KIPLMC2, choosing N≍dθ/ε2N\asymp d_\theta/\varepsilon^2N≍dθ​/ε2 gives

N(dθ+Ndx)≍dθε1+dxε2.\sqrt{N(d_\theta+Nd_x)} \asymp\frac{d_\theta}{\varepsilon} \sqrt{1+\frac{d_x}{\varepsilon^2}}.N(dθ​+Ndx​)​≍εdθ​​1+ε2dx​​​.

To make the persistent numerical error of order ε\varepsilonε, take the minimum of the stability threshold and ε/N(dθ+Ndx)\varepsilon/\sqrt{N(d_\theta+Nd_x)}ε/N(dθ​+Ndx​)​. In the small-error regime this is a step of order ε3/(dθdx)\varepsilon^3/(d_\theta\sqrt{d_x})ε3/(dθ​dx​​). Both transient terms can then be controlled after O~(dθdx/ε3)\widetilde O(d_\theta\sqrt{d_x}/\varepsilon^3)O(dθ​dx​​/ε3) steps, provided the initial transport error grows at most polynomially in particle number and dimension so that its logarithm remains in the suppressed factor.

The manuscript also studies logistic regression, Wisconsin cancer data, a Bayesian neural network, a multi-well model and runtime comparisons. Its signed weighted area between error curves is ∑i=1M2i(cIPLA(i)−cKIPLMC2(i))/(M(M+1))\sum_{i=1}^M2i(c^{\mathrm{IPLA}}(i)-c^{\mathrm{KIPLMC2}}(i))/(M(M+1))∑i=1M​2i(cIPLA(i)−cKIPLMC2(i))/(M(M+1)). Positive values favor KIPLMC2 by this metric. Its predictive log score averages the log probability assigned to each correct test label.

These are empirical comparisons with concrete data and numerical settings. The strong-convexity convergence theorems, their asymptotic complexity corollaries, the algorithm definitions and the experimental metrics are different kinds of content. The logistic example is globally smooth and can be strictly convex under a full-span feature condition, while common-translation directions still prevent a positive uniform strong-convexity constant without additional regularization.

The statistical choice of particle count first fixes the dimension-dependent numerical coefficient. The discretization-error bound then fixes a step, and the contraction rate fixes the iteration count. Empirical advantages at particular model settings remain separate from these global sufficient conditions, especially when a model lacks uniform joint strong convexity.

The finite error allocations and source dimension identity are proved. Reported numerical traces and timing measurements remain empirical observations, not mathematical universal claims.

Compile and verify

git clone https://github.com/odakyildiz/LangevinLean.git
cd LangevinLean
lake exe cache get
lake build KIPLMC
lake env lean KIPLMC/Check.lean
bash scripts/check-local.sh

Reproduce the formal proof

Install Git and elan, Lean’s toolchain manager, before cloning. The repository pins the Lean and Mathlib versions. The first cache download requires an internet connection.

lake build checks the Lean proofs. The audit file prints the logical axioms used by the results. The local check script also verifies that every displayed source excerpt matches the repository and that the mathematical pages regenerate correctly. Documentation generation requires Python 3 and Node.js.
